newsitem.title: USA: Most Californians on aid can weather reform - study.
newsitem.headline: Most Californians on aid can weather reform - study.

text.p: While many California families on public assistance will be hard hit by welfare reform, the vast majority of them should be able to cope with the changes, according to a study released on Tuesday.

A study by the Public Policy Institute of California found that about one-third of all California families -- nearly 4.5 million -- receive some form of public assistance, and one-quarter participate in a major welfare program.
Nearly 500,000 of these families could be hit hard by welfare reform, the study concluded.
"How long a family is on welfare is not nearly as important as how dependent they are on the system," said economist Thomas MaCurdy, who headed the study.

The study said that the typical recipient family receives six percent of its annual income from welfare programs including Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC), Food Stamps, Supplemental Security Income and Medi-Cal.

Nearly one-fourth of all participants receive only Medi-Cal, no cash benefits. Less than a third of all welfare families take part in AFDC and two-thirds of those families had additional income sources, including earnings from work.
Because the vast majority of families on assistance are not highly dependent on the welfare they receive, they should be able to handle welfare reform, the study concluded.

However, the study found that about 45 percent of all families receiving Aid to Families with Dependent Children -- 432,000 -- are "highly dependent" on welfare programs. An estimated 262,000 of those families have no income other than public assistance, the study said.
In addition, of the half million immigrants who receive welfare benefits, 281,000 families could be affected by the welfare changes, the study found.

Recent immigrants have high rates of welfare participation, nearly twice that of other families. The study found that 20,000 of those families are likely to suffer a 50 to 80 percent reduction in income because of the reforms.
The non-profit Public Policy Institute of California said its study was based on data from 1993 and 1994 and a sample of more than 5,000 California families.
